newsitem.title: BURUNDI: Defiant Burundi rejects talks while embargo stays.
newsitem.headline: Defiant Burundi rejects talks while embargo stays.

text.p: Burundi's military regime defied regional leaders on Monday by refusing to negotiate with Hutu rebels until economic sanctions are lifted.
Prime Minister Pascal Firmin Ndimira told diplomats the embargo was "a rope around the government's neck".
"The blockade is an obstacle and the government cannot dialogue until it is lifted," Ndimira told the meeting at a Bujumbura hotel which reporters attended.
The total trade and transport embargo was maintained at a regional summit last Saturday.
It was imposed on landlocked Burundi on July 31 as punishment for the military coup six days earlier which installed Major Pierre Buyoya in power.

Regional states, fearing the ethnic war between the rebels and the mainly Tutsi army is leading to catastrophe, justified the sanctions as a means of forcing the dominant Tutsi minority to share power with the Hutu majority.

Killings by the rebels, the army, militias and even ordinary villagers are going on every day. Human rights workers believe the toll is running at several hundreds of people each month. Diplomats, U.N. staff and most aid agencies are restricted to the capital because of insecurity in the interior.
The few aid workers in the interior who are witnessing horrors are afraid to publicise them, knowing they could be expelled or even killed themselves.
At their latest summit the regional leaders gave Buyoya one month to enter negotiations with Leonard Nyangoma's Forces for the Defence of Democracy (FDD) and smaller Hutu armed factions.
Ndimira, a civilian and a Hutu, delivered a clear reply from Buyoya and the army colonels who backed him, saying the sanctions were illegal, unfair and were causing a humanitarian crisis in Burundi.
He said they imperilled the peace process by helping the rebels and he accused unspecified leaders of plotting against Burundi.
"The government again announces its willingness to enter negotiations with the armed factions," Ndimira said. But they could not begin while the embargo lasted, he added.
Buyoya has previously agreed to unconditional talks with the rebels but Monday's change of heart seemed linked to his failure to get sanctions eased.
Smuggling and ethnic sympathies between Burundians and their neighbours in Rwanda, Tanzania and Zaire mean basic commodities, such as oil, are getting in.
But exports of coffee and tea have virtually dried up and the regime is eating into its foreign reserves.
The real issue is the order to enter serious negotiations with the rebels, diplomats say. Tutsi hardliners in and out of uniform are flatly opposed to real power-sharing talks with Nyangoma.
They say the former interior minister is from the same mould as the Hutu politicians in Rwanda who organised the 1994 genocide of up to one million minority Tutsis and pro-opposition Hutus.
Diplomats say Buyoya might be forced to quit if he accepted talks with Nyangoma, whether or not sanctions are in place.
